name: George Soros
role: Investor and philanthropist; founder of the Open Society Foundations
summary: Soros describes his outlook as a defence of the open society, the idea from Karl Popper that no one has perfect knowledge and that free speech and free elections are preferable to imposed ideology. He criticises market fundamentalism, supports closer European integration and the euro's reform, and opposes authoritarian governments, especially China under Xi Jinping. His stated positions on most economic and social statements are not recorded in the sources reviewed.

sources.title: George Soros

sources.title: The 'Mortal Danger' of China's Push Into AI
sources.author: Tom Simonite, Wired (reprinted at tibet.net)
sources.usedFor: Report of his January 2019 Davos speech: 'mortal threat to open societies' from AI and surveillance in the hands of repressive regimes

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In a 2009 lecture he rejects the efficient-market view and its political form, market fundamentalism, which assumes markets correct themselves without government intervention. He does not deny that markets allocate resources.

strong-leader.rationale: He calls Xi Jinping a dictator who uses technology to impose total control and whose regime is opposed to open-society values; Wikipedia reports his description of Donald Trump as a con man. He does not address gridlock directly.

abortion-legal.rationale: In a July 2022 Project Syndicate column he wrote that Congress must act, 'starting with protecting a woman's right to choose'.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In 2015 he wrote that the EU 'has to accept at least a million asylum-seekers annually for the foreseeable future' and urged a single EU asylum agency. He did not address immigration levels generally.

open-borders.rationale: Wikipedia quotes him contrasting Orban's plan, which treats national borders as the objective, with his own, which treats national borders as the obstacle. In 2015 he also called for 'effective governance over the flows of asylum-seekers', so the evidence points both ways.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: He warns that human civilization is in danger of collapse from climate change and that change is nearing irreversibility. He names no specific government measure.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: He calls the threat from new technology in the hands of authoritarians 'a mortal threat to open societies'. He does not argue that technology will solve most problems.

democracy-best.rationale: He prefers a society with free speech and free elections to one that imposes its ideology by force, but also says free political discourse does not necessarily produce more far-sighted policies than an authoritarian regime.

accelerate-technology.rationale: He treats AI and surveillance technology as a danger to open societies when repressive regimes control it. He does not address speeding up technological change in general.

algorithmic-government.rationale: He warns that machine learning and AI can give repressive regimes instruments of control. He does not address algorithmic decision-making in democratic governments.

reason-over-faith.rationale: No stated position on reason as the only guide; saying people need beliefs is something nearby.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: He calls for a single EU asylum and migration agency and, in a 2011 open letter he drafted, for a common EU treasury and fiscal supervision. In 2022 he praised the EU's response to Ukraine.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Wikipedia reports that in 2015 he called Putin's annexation of Crimea a challenge to the prevailing world order. He does not address occupation or its legal status.

common-currency.rationale: He says the euro 'has many unresolved problems' that 'must not be allowed to destroy the European Union', and that a fully-fledged currency needs a central bank and a treasury. He backs the single currency while calling for its design to be fixed.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: No stated position on courts constraining majorities; urging voters to elect a different party to rein in the Court is something nearby.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He calls China and Russia the greatest threats to open societies and, per Wikipedia, called the Hungarian government 'a mafia state' after its campaign against his foundations.

assisted-dying.rationale: Wikipedia reports that in a 1994 speech he said he had offered to help his mother end her life, endorsed Oregon's Death with Dignity Act and helped fund its advertising.

person-over-state.rationale: In 2022 he wrote that in an open society 'the role of the state is to protect the freedom of the individual'. He did not use the wording of this statement.

close-ties-china.rationale: He calls China and Russia 'the greatest threats to open societies', says Xi appeared to give Putin room to invade Ukraine, and urges Europe to hold China accountable.

notes: Coverage is thin. The full texts of The Crisis of Global Capitalism (1998), Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000) and The Capitalist Threat (Atlantic, 1997) could not be opened (lending-library restriction; Atlantic site blocked). Most Project Syndicate columns and the 2022 Wall Street Journal op-ed are paywalled, so only their opening sections were read. Positions on drug policy (the 2010 Proposition 19 op-ed), the death penalty, taxes, welfare and trade are therefore null: the only evidence found was donations or was reported only in search snippets, which were not opened. Davos 2018 and 2019 texts were not available in full; the 2019 speech is covered through a Wired report. Several answers rest on Wikipedia quotes of his statements, which are marked reference and given low or medium confidence where the original was not read.
